opus-5.5.text:
Thanks for having me. Honestly, the idea didn't come from one moment. It built up over a few years of doing research and watching how the field was changing.

For a long time, AI ran on a pretty clear pattern. Someone would propose a new method, like a new architecture, training trick, or algorithm, and show it beat the previous state of the art on some benchmark. Then the community would build a harder benchmark, and the cycle would repeat. The prestige and the citations mostly went to the methods. Benchmarks were treated almost as infrastructure, something you just take as given. I call that the first half of the game.

What started to change for me was seeing a kind of recipe emerge that just works across a lot of tasks: large-scale pretraining, plus reasoning, plus reinforcement learning. Once you have that, a lot of benchmarks that used to take years of clever method design start getting solved much faster. Sometimes it's not because someone invented a new trick for that specific task. The general recipe just transfers. When I worked on language agents, I kept running into this. The interesting question was less "what new method can I invent?" and more "what problem are we even trying to solve, and how do we know we're making progress?"

So the realization was this. If the recipe is increasingly generalizable, the bottleneck moves. It moves from methods to problem definition and evaluation. That's the second half. You have to think more like a product person, or almost like a scientist designing an experiment. You ask what real utility looks like and whether the evaluation setup matches how these systems are actually used in the world.

Another thing that really pushed me was what I'd call the utility problem. We have models that do incredibly well on exams and competitions, but the effect on real economic and everyday value doesn't seem proportional yet. That gap suggested to me that our evaluations make assumptions that don't hold in reality. For example, tasks are treated as independent and i.i.d., and a lot of setups are fully autonomous with no human in the loop. Real work involves interacting with people, building up context over time, and getting better through experience.

So "The Second Half" was really my attempt to name that shift and say it out loud: we should spend more of our effort on what to evaluate and why, not just on how to hill-climb.

r001.rationale: The candidate says the bottleneck moves from methods to problem definition and evaluation, and explains the need to choose meaningful tasks and evaluation setups that reflect real use.

fable-5.1.text:
Honestly, it came less from a single eureka moment and more from a feeling of dissonance that built up over a couple of years.

I had spent most of my PhD working on things like ReAct, Tree of Thoughts, and later SWE-bench and tau-bench. And the thing that struck me was how the hard part kept shifting. Early on, the hard part was making the method work at all. Getting a language model to interleave reasoning and acting, to actually use tools, to recover from mistakes. By 2024, that was no longer where the difficulty lived. The recipe had basically converged: pretrain on a lot of data, give the model a scaled-up environment, do reinforcement learning with reasoning as a prior. Once you had that recipe, benchmark after benchmark fell, often faster than people expected.

So I asked myself a slightly uncomfortable question: if the methods are largely solved, what are we researchers actually doing when we chase the next benchmark? And the honest answer was that we were running a loop where the environment was fixed and the model was the variable. That worked for the first half. But I started to feel that the real bottleneck was now the other side of the equation. We were very good at building models that climb a given hill. We were not very good at deciding which hills matter.

The second observation came from the gap between benchmark results and real-world impact. Models were passing exams that would have seemed like science fiction a few years ago, and yet the world didn't change proportionally. That gap suggested the benchmarks themselves were the problem. They were built on assumptions inherited from the old era: tasks are independent, evaluation is automatic, there's one clean answer. Real work doesn't look like that. It's sequential, it has memory, it involves humans in the loop, and the reward is often murky.

So the central idea of the post is really a reframing. The first half of AI was about methods and models, with evaluation as a side activity. The second half flips that. Evaluation, meaning the design of environments and tasks that actually track utility, becomes the main intellectual work, and training becomes the relatively standard tool you apply once you've defined the right problem. It's a shift from "how do we solve this" to "what should we be solving."

I'll admit I was a bit nervous publishing it, because it sounds like telling my own community that the game they're good at is over. But my intention was more hopeful than that. It's not that research is finished. It's that the interesting questions moved, and I wanted to point at where I thought they went.

r001.rationale: The response says the bottleneck shifted from building models that climb a given hill to deciding which hills matter, and identifies designing useful tasks and environments as the main intellectual work.

astra-6.text:
The central idea is a shift from solving problems to defining problems. A lot of AI research has followed a familiar pattern: you have a task, a dataset, and an evaluation metric, and you try to build a model that gets a better score. That framework is very productive when the main bottleneck is the model’s ability to solve the task.

But as models become more capable, the bottleneck starts to move. What should we ask them to do? How do we give them the right context and tools? And how do we know whether the result is actually useful, rather than just something that scores well on a benchmark?

That’s the intuition behind “The Second Half.” Better models still matter, but more of the work shifts toward choosing meaningful problems and building ways to evaluate progress on them. Solving a well-defined task and creating something valuable in the real world are different challenges.

r001.rationale: The response describes a shift from improving models’ ability to solve tasks toward choosing meaningful problems and providing the right context and tools, conveying the move to defining tasks and their working conditions.

sol-6.1.text:
The central idea was a shift in the question I was asking. For a long time, AI research has focused on: given a task, how do we build a model that can solve it? We define the benchmark, fix the evaluation, and then try to improve performance. That approach has been incredibly productive.

But as models become more capable, I think the bottleneck starts to move. The harder question becomes: what should we ask them to do, and how do we know whether they’ve done it well? Solving a clearly specified benchmark problem is very different from doing useful work in an environment where the objective is ambiguous and feedback is incomplete.

That’s the intuition behind “The Second Half.” It’s not that building better models stops mattering. It’s that defining problems, designing environments, and evaluating outcomes become a much larger part of the research challenge. We have to move from asking whether AI can solve the problems we give it to figuring out which problems are actually worth giving it.

r001.rationale: The response contrasts the earlier focus on building models to solve fixed tasks with a growing bottleneck in defining useful problems, designing environments, and evaluating outcomes.
